title: Caching strategies: cache-aside (lazy load), write-through (write to cache + DB together), write-behind (write to cache, async to DB), cache invalidation (TTL, event-based), thundering herd / cache stampede prevention.
keyPoints: Cache-aside (lazy loading) checks the cache on read, loads from the database on a miss, and populates the cache for future reads.
Write-through writes to both the cache and database together, keeping the cache always consistent but with slightly slower writes.
Write-behind writes to the cache immediately and flushes to the database asynchronously, risking data loss on cache crash.
TTL-based invalidation expires entries after a fixed duration, simple but allows brief staleness.
Event-based invalidation deletes or updates the cache entry the instant the underlying data changes, precise but requires wiring.
Cache stampede (thundering herd) happens when a hot key expires and many requests miss simultaneously; prevent with single-flight locks.
For banking balances, use write-through with event-based invalidation for correctness; use write-behind only for tolerant data like analytics.

s1_definition.oneliner: Cache-aside loads lazily, write-through writes both, write-behind writes later, invalidation keeps it fresh, and a single-flight lock stops a stampede.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Cache-aside (lazy loading)** : on a read, the application checks the cache; on a miss it loads from the database and populates the cache, so only requested data is cached.
- **Write-through** : writes to the cache and the database together on every write, so the cache is always consistent with the database.
- **Write-behind (write-back)** : writes to the cache immediately and queues the database write to happen asynchronously, trading durability for speed.
- **Cache invalidation** : keeping cached entries fresh via time-to-live (TTL) or event-based deletion when the underlying data changes.
- **Cache stampede (thundering herd)** : when a popular key expires and many requests miss the cache simultaneously and all slam the database; prevented with a single-flight lock or probabilistic early expiration.
s1_definition.analogy: The teller at National Bank of India keeps a note of Rajesh's balance on the desk so they do not walk to the vault every time. Cache-aside means the teller fetches from the vault only when the note is missing. Write-through means whenever the balance changes, the teller updates both the note and the vault book together. Write-behind means the teller updates the note instantly and writes to the vault book later. Invalidation means tearing up an outdated note. Stampede prevention means that when many tellers need the same missing note at once, only one walks to the vault while the others wait for the answer.

```text
  Cache-Aside (Lazy Load)           Write-Through
  ┌────────┐  1. GET   ┌───────┐   ┌────────┐  1. WRITE  ┌───────┐
  │  App   │─────────►│ Cache │   │  App   │──────────►│ Cache │
  └────┬───┘  2. MISS  └───┬───┘   └────┬───┘           └───┬───┘
       │                   │            │  2. WRITE         │
       │  3. LOAD          │            │                   │
       ▼                   │            ▼                   │
  ┌────────┐               │       ┌────────┐              │
  │   DB   │───────────────┘       │   DB   │──────────────┘
  └────────┘  4. POPULATE cache    └────────┘  Both updated together

  Write-Behind                      Stampede Prevention
  ┌────────┐  1. WRITE  ┌───────┐   ┌──────┐  MISS  ┌───────┐  MISS
  │  App   │──────────►│ Cache │   │ Req1 │──────►│ Cache │◄──── Req2
  └────────┘           └───┬───┘   └──┬───┘       └───────┘     Req3
                           │          │ gets lock               wait
                    async  │          ▼
                           │     ┌────────┐
                           ▼     │   DB   │  only ONE DB call
                      ┌────────┐ └────┬───┘
                      │   DB   │      │ populate cache
                      └────────┘      ▼
                      (may lose data  all requests served
                       on crash)      from fresh cache)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Caching strategies define how an application reads from and writes to a cache relative to its backing database, and I pick them per data type rather than applying one everywhere. For reads, cache-aside, or lazy loading, is my default: on a read I check the cache, and on a miss I load from the database and populate the cache, so only requested data is cached. Its weakness is that the first read is slow and the cache can go stale after a write, so I always pair it with an invalidation strategy.

For writes, I choose between write-through and write-behind by how much I value correctness versus latency. Write-through writes to the cache and database together, so the cache is never stale, at the cost of a slightly slower write; this is my default for bank balances, where a wrong value is unacceptable. Write-behind writes to the cache immediately and flushes to the database asynchronously, which is very fast and batchable but loses recent writes if the cache crashes before flushing, so I use it only for tolerant data like analytics counters, never for money.

Invalidation keeps the cache honest. A time-to-live expires entries automatically so staleness self-heals after a bounded delay, which is simple but allows brief staleness. Event-based invalidation deletes or updates the entry the instant the underlying data changes, which is precise and what I use for balances so that right after a transfer at National Bank of India, the next read reflects the new balance rather than the old one.

The subtle failure I always design for is the thundering herd, or cache stampede. When a very popular key like the current interest rate expires, a flood of requests can miss simultaneously and all slam the database at once. I prevent this with a single-flight lock so only one request rebuilds the value while the others wait, and I complement it with staggered or probabilistic early expiration so hot keys refresh just before they fully expire.

Remember one sentence: pick caching strategies per data type : write-through for money, cache-aside for reads, stampede protection for hot keys, and never write-behind for anything you cannot afford to lose.
